title: The Brass Crab's Whistle
markdown:
The lane behind St Jude’s held a peculiar quiet. Sunlight lingered on the cobbles like spilled honey, even when cloud covered the rest of the town. Elias Thorne polished a stubbornly dull spanner and tried, as usual, to look like a man who had planned his afternoon.

A scrabble came from the workshop’s depths, then a whirlwind of boots.

“Mr Thorne. You won’t believe this.”

Pip Featherbottom skidded to a halt, a hummingbird of restless energy in a too-large apron. They thrust forward a tarnished object: a tiny brass crab, legs tucked, a whistle like a misplaced antenna.

Elias did not look up. The air smelled of oil and the particular impatience of apprentices. “Another pebble that looks like a stoic badger?”

“Under the old sundial by the church wall. It was just there. It feels buzzy. Like a trapped bee.”

He took it. Old, older than any clock he had mended, etched with marks no local maker used. He was about to explain oxidation in a sensible voice when Pip, unable to leave a whistle unblown, set their mouth to it.

A note escaped, thin as a dragonfly’s sigh.

The world did not jolt. It swirled, liquid and polite, as if the lane had been stirred with a spoon. Oil and dust became damp earth and woodsmoke. Tools blurred into rough wood. The light outside thickened, yellow as old butter.

“Pip,” Elias said, and the word came out tighter than a nut. “What did you do?”

Pip pointed. The workshop door was planked. A woman in homespun led a very large, very woolly sheep past a cottage that had decided to be mud.

“That sheep wasn’t there a second ago. And I think that’s Mrs Higgins’s place. Smaller. And made of… well.”

The crab hummed in Elias’s palm, warm as a just-used key. Distant carts. Bleating. Voices in a clipped older English, laid over the lane like a second map.

“Right.” He clutched the spanner, a familiar weight. “Patience. All will be revealed in time. Or we have been revealed in it. Highly irregular.” A breath. “The whistle folded the lane. Somewhere. Somewhen.”

Pip grinned, which was not the approved response. “A time-slip. We’re adventurers.”

“We are temporarily misplaced individuals. And you caused it. We need to get back before anything else is filed under the wrong century.”

They stepped onto a muddy track churned by hooves. The church spire looked a little less sure of itself. A smell of wet wool and woodsmoke replaced every familiar oil-note. Elias turned a loose crab-leg between finger and thumb. “If we cannot send ourselves home, we may have to learn to knit sheep for a living. I am not,” he added, “qualified.”

Pip’s bravado thinned at a signpost: To Meadow. To Market. The letters were cut deeper than Oakhaven’s enamel plates, as if time had more patience. A man in tunic and hose stared as if they had grown spare heads. Pip, against all instruction, waved. The man muttered something about mad folk and hurried on.

“We stick out like oil on a tapestry,” Elias hissed. “Sensible. Blend.”

“We haven’t got tunics. And I don’t think they do carburetors.” Pip crouched to look at a hoofprint the size of a dinner plate. “Also the sheep are taking the job seriously.”

Near a wattle cottage, a hooded figure stood in an oak’s shade with a stillness that was not rest. Elias’s mechanic mind, which preferred faults you could oil, labelled it a threat and then, more honestly, a problem.

The figure melted away.

“New plan. Understand the crab. Avoid that. Pip, the sundial. Anything else?”

Pip bit their lip. “A carving. A wave. A ripple. I kicked a loose stone and the crab was under it.”

One crab-leg sat askew, like a wave about to break. Elias wiggled it. Nothing. Then he saw a pinprick indentation beside the joint, a keyhole too small for any honest key.

The hooded figure returned, closer, holding something long and thin that caught the thick light. A tuning fork.

“Stop, you children,” rasped a voice like dry leaves. “You have what does not belong to you. You have disturbed the balance.”

Pip stepped in front of Elias, which was brave and also not in the workshop rules. “We found it.”

“Found, or given by the careless hand of time? It sings a song of wrongness. Your modern noise has spoiled the harmony.”

Elias looked from Pip to crab to fork. Sundial wave. Loose stone. Loose leg. The connection arrived the way a stubborn bolt sometimes does: all at once, after you have stopped forcing it.

“The leg isn’t broken. It’s meant to turn.”

He turned it. A click, soft and satisfied. The indentation widened. Inside, on faded velvet, lay a single smooth grey pebble, the sort a child might skip and then forget.

The figure gasped. “The Anchor Stone.”

“It looks like a boring grey rock,” Pip said.

“A stabiliser,” Elias murmured. The pebble was cool. “To stop the thing drifting. You can start the song. We can hold the quiet. It seems we are inconveniently necessary to each other.”

The hood fell back. The face was old, parchment-thin, eyes bright with knowledge and a kind of desperate courtesy. “I am Elara. Guardian of the Temporal Currents in this localised anomaly. The crab is a Chrono-Resonator. The stone is its silence. Without it, arrivals become… messy. Like yours.”

Pip looked sheepish. “So I made a bit of a mess.”

“A temporal one,” Elias said. He held out the stone. “If you can wake it, we can put it back to sleep.”

Elara nodded. “Song and silence. Ebb and flow.”

They stood in the oak’s shade: mechanic, apprentice, guardian. Pip took the crab. Elara raised the fork.

“When it rings, blow, and think of home,” Elara said. “Elias, hold the stone. Feel its stillness. Do not rush it.”

She struck the fork on the ancient oak. A pure note went through bone and lane and the idea of now. The crab answered from inside.

“Now, Pip.”

Pip blew. The whistle came out stronger, laced with oil and honeyed cobbles and a dull spanner left on a bench. The cottage wavered. The lane dissolved. Elara’s face stretched like wet paper.

A last light appeared on the windows of a far hill, ordinary as a kitchen lamp.

“Hold steady,” Elara said, already thinning. “Remember the quiet.”

Elias gripped the pebble until his fingers ached. Pip blew until their cheeks shook. The fork’s hum soared and cut off.

Oil. Dust. The workshop, exactly as left. The spanner still dull. Elias opened his hand. The Anchor Stone was gone. The crab lay inert in Pip’s palm, a brass ornament with no opinion.

“We’re back,” Pip said, wonder worn down to tiredness.

Elias laughed once, shaky, and looked at them without the usual inventory of hazards. “You were remarkably composed. For an adventurer. The whistle had more conviction than the paperwork allowed.”

Pip flushed, then set the crab on the shelf beside a jar of bent pins, as if it had always belonged with the useful junk. Outside, the lane kept its honeyed quiet. Elias picked up the spanner, then put it down again, and left the workbench one degree less tidy than his principles preferred. The sundial by the church wall threw a shadow that did not quite match the hour. Neither of them mentioned it. The afternoon, which had been so determined to be sensible, went on smelling of oil, and of a pebble that had stayed behind.
characters: Elias Thorne (reserved mechanic who is trying very hard to seem sensible), Pip (a junior member desperate to prove themselves)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, fantastic story for curious young teens
